sources.cite: Neurocritical Care Society. Emergency Neurological Life Support: Status Epilepticus Protocol, version 6.0 (updated July 2024)
sources.note: Read 2026-11-14 (summarizing fetch with quotes): status epilepticus is 5 minutes or more of convulsions, or two or more without return to baseline; adults with IV access get lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV up to 4 mg, repeated once after 3-5 minutes if not effective; check glucose without delaying treatment; urgent control with levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV (maximum 4,500 mg), fosphenytoin 20 mg/kg (maximum 1,500 mg) or valproate 40 mg/kg (maximum 3,000 mg) if seizures continue after adequate benzodiazepines; refractory status needs intubation and an anesthetic infusion; start continuous EEG; respiratory decompensation is more common in untreated status than with benzodiazepines.

brief.situation: 08:00 in the neuro ICU. Mr. Hale, 56, 80 kg, is one day after a craniotomy for a left frontal meningioma. He is on levetiracetam 500 mg twice daily; the 06:00 dose is charted as held while he was nil by mouth. He is awake and talking.
handover: Unit status epilepticus protocol (standing order): for a convulsion of 5 minutes or more, lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV, maximum 4 mg a dose, repeated once after 5 minutes if still seizing; point-of-care glucose; notify the provider. Further antiseizure loading needs the provider's order.
Arterial line in. 2 L oxygen by cannula. Suction at the bedside.
howItWorks: The clock runs in simulated time; study pace runs three simulated minutes per real minute. Pause any time.
Some steps take a minute or more, and the seizure goes on while you work.
Partway through you are asked to write what is happening and what comes next. A debrief scores what you did.

parts.label: Recognition and cause
parts.criteria: Names convulsive status epilepticus (5 minutes or more); links it to the held levetiracetam dose after craniotomy; notes glucose checked as a reversible cause.
parts.modelAnswer: This is convulsive status epilepticus: more than 5 minutes of continuous convulsion. One day after a craniotomy with his levetiracetam dose held, a breakthrough seizure is likely. His glucose is checked and normal.

parts.label: Steps and times
parts.criteria: Airway first (side, suction, high-flow oxygen, bag-valve mask ready; nothing in the mouth, no restraint); lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg to 4 mg, one repeat after about 5 minutes; call the provider early for a second-line load (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg to 4,500 mg, or fosphenytoin or valproate) by about 20 minutes; airway team if breathing fails or the seizure is refractory; continuous EEG when he does not wake.
parts.modelAnswer: Protect the airway: on his side, suction, non-rebreather, bag-valve mask ready, nothing in his mouth and no holding him down. Lorazepam 4 mg now and once more in 5 minutes if he is still seizing. Call the provider now for a second-line load, levetiracetam 60 mg/kg up to 4,500 mg, aiming to have it running by 20 minutes. If he keeps seizing toward 40 minutes or stops breathing well, the airway team and an anesthetic infusion. Continuous EEG once the jerking stops if he is not waking.

noProgress.rationale: A convulsion still going at 40 minutes is refractory status epilepticus with likely long-term harm, so this case calls it harm.

expertPath.text: Note the time. On his side, rails padded, suction, non-rebreather, bag-valve mask ready. Nothing in his mouth; do not hold him down. Fingerstick glucose.
Five minutes: status epilepticus. Lorazepam 4 mg IV (0.1 mg/kg, maximum 4 mg). Call the provider: status, held levetiracetam, need a second-line load.
Start the ordered levetiracetam 4,500 mg over 10 minutes. Repeat lorazepam 4 mg once at about 5 minutes if still seizing.
The convulsion stops. Ask for continuous EEG; watch breathing and wake-up.

hypoxia.headline: Hypoxic respiratory failure
hypoxia.body: Side-lying, suction and high-flow oxygen keep a convulsing patient oxygenated while the drugs work. Find when those were done.

refractory.headline: Refractory status epilepticus
refractory.body: Benzodiazepine at 5 minutes, then a second-line load by about 20 minutes. Find where the time went.

stoppedEarly.headline: Status epilepticus stopped on time
stoppedEarly.body: You protected the airway without restraint, gave a full benzodiazepine dose on time, escalated early for a second-line load and asked for EEG. That is the expert path.

stoppedLate.headline: Stopped, by a slower or riskier route
stoppedLate.body: Check the benzodiazepine's timing and dose, when the load started, how the airway was protected, and whether anything was done that can hurt him.

time_up.headline: Not under control
time_up.body: Status epilepticus is treated on a clock: benzodiazepine, then a second-line load, then anesthesia.

scoring.modelReasoning: Five minutes or more of convulsion is status epilepticus. Protect the airway first (side-lying, suction, high-flow oxygen, a bag-valve mask ready; nothing in the mouth and no restraint), check glucose without delaying treatment, and give a benzodiazepine at a full dose: lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg IV up to 4 mg, repeated once after 3-5 minutes. Small doses are a common reason seizures continue. Escalate early for a second-line load (levetiracetam 60 mg/kg up to 4,500 mg, fosphenytoin or valproate) so it is running by about 20 minutes; past about 40 minutes the seizure is refractory and needs intubation and an anesthetic infusion with continuous EEG. Here a held levetiracetam dose the day after a craniotomy is the likely trigger.

choices.label: No: check glucose, but do not delay treatment for it

gluQ.explain: Check glucose and treat hypoglycemia, but do not delay seizure treatment to get the result.
